newsitem.title: USA: Quaker's Snapple sale raises questions about Gatorade.
newsitem.headline: Quaker's Snapple sale raises questions about Gatorade.

text.p: Quaker Oats Co.'s sale of its Snapple beverage business for a loss of $1.4 billion raises questions about the fate of its crown jewel, Gatorade, and of long-time Chairman William Smithburg.
"Quaker Oats has to continue to explore other alternatives to improve their profile," CS First Boston analyst Michael Mauboussin said.
One option, Mauboussin added, would be to spin off all or part of Gatorade sports drink, Quaker's single biggest brand, which generated $1.4 billion in sales in 1996.

Market rumors persist that Quaker may consider selling Gatorade, although the company would face a large tax liability if that business were sold. Quaker had been rumored to be seeking as much as $3.5 billion to $4 billion for Gatorade.
Quaker Oats spokesman Ronald Bottrell declined to comment on rumors related to Gatorade, which Quaker Oats acquired in 1983 when it bought Stokely-Van Camp for $238 million.

Gatorade, which had only $90 million in sales when it was acquired, has been hailed as a successful acquisition for Quaker. Considering the $120 million in cash that Stokely-Van Camp had on its books and the money Quaker has received in sales of some Stokely-Van Camp businesses, "we got Gatorade for free," Bottrell said.

While Quaker management has given no hints about the future of any of its businesses -- nor did the company comment about persistent rumors that Snapple was going to be sold -- the chairman has repeatedly said he is committed to creating value for shareholders.

"As I have said before, we actively and diligently seek ways to create that value and consider all options," Smithburg said in a speech to financial analysts last month. "That's my responsibility to shareholders of this company. My intensity directed at achieving that goal is greater than it has ever been. Value is our only goal."
Smithburg said last week that the decision to sell Snapple to Triarc Cos. Inc. for $300 million was reached after a review of "various shareholder value-building options by management."
The company added it expected to recoup taxes on previous capital gains of about $250 million, making the cash value of the Snapple deal about $550 million.

That is still far less than the total of $1.8 billion, including acquisition costs, that Quaker paid for Snapple in late 1994. At that time, Smithburg faced criticism that the price paid for Snapple was too high.

"People laughed at the price he paid in 1994. (The Snapple deal) started out wrong and just got worse," said James Schrager, senior lecturer in business policy at the University of Chicago, Graduate School of Business. "How he (Smithburg) is going to survive this is going to be interesting."

However, Schrager, who is also president of the Great Lakes Group Inc. consulting firm, noted that Smithburg has the advantage of a long career at the company and an undoubtedly loyal board. Smithburg, 58, has been chairman and chief executive officer at Quaker since 1983.

Now, the challenge remains for Smithburg and Quaker management to maximize profits from remaining businesses, which include oatmeal, which is benefiting from health claims that oat bran helps reduce the risk of heart disease; ready-to-eat cereals like Cap'n Crunch and Life, and Rice A Roni rice side dishes.
But it may provide difficult for Quaker to squeeze more efficiencies out of its remaining businesses, said Goldman Sachs analyst Nomi Ghez.
"I have to believe over the past two years that they really tried to improve the profitability of their other businesses" to offset some of the losses from Snapple, Ghez said.
